how to improve GPT-6 Astra / Codex's ability to design and code websites

I've been using this approach since GPT Image was released, and the results have kept improving with 2 and 2.5

the idea is to have Codex generate visual mockups of the website before building it, whether you're reimagining an existing page or starting with an idea from scratch

you can review the layout, give feedback and agree on the design before it starts writing the frontend

here's how to use it:

1. give Codex the idea and your context

explain who the website is for, what it needs to communicate and what you want someone to do when they visit

include the material you already have:

> your page copy and product information
> brand guidelines, fonts, colors and assets
> screenshots of the existing page if you're redesigning
> references with notes on what you like about each one

have it ask about anything missing before generating the mockup

for an existing website, ask it to inspect the current implementation too, including components and functionality that need to stay

2. ask it to generate the design first

be explicit that you want an image mockup to review before implementation

a starting prompt:

> use imagegen to create a website mockup from this brief and the attached references
> use the supplied copy, brand assets and product information
> show the page layout, typography, imagery and calls to action, and wait for my feedback before writing code

you can request different visual directions if you're still exploring, with each version changing something meaningful like the layout or use of imagery

3. work through the mockup together

review it as a page someone needs to understand and use

> is the main message clear?
> does the layout guide attention toward the intended action?
> is the text readable?
> does the design fit your brand?
> are there generic sections or invented details that should be removed?

give specific feedback on the image, such as increasing the space around the headline, reducing decorative elements or moving the product example higher on the page

ask it to revise the chosen mockup while preserving the parts you've approved

4. turn the approved mockup into a build plan

have Codex identify the sections, reusable components and assets needed to implement the design

agree on what happens when someone interacts with it, including navigation, forms, buttons and any loading or error states

also define how the layout should adapt to mobile, because a desktop mockup leaves those decisions open

save the approved image and your decisions in the project so Codex can refer to them during the build

5. find relevant UX / UI skills before building

you can find these in skill directories and through recommendations on X, UI Skills is one example to explore

https://t.co/NSjtzraOfs

give your Grok Bot the project brief and have it research which skills are popular and worth considering for your stack

ask it to check what each skill does, who maintains it and whether its instructions fit the website you're building

that could include skills for:

> frontend design and component patterns
> accessibility and responsive layouts
> animation and interaction design
> reviewing the finished UI

review the shortlist, then give Codex the selected skills alongside your design system and approved mockup before implementation

6. build the page from that reference

ask Codex to implement the approved design using your project's existing stack and components where appropriate

keep headings, buttons and forms as working website elements, with illustrations and other generated visuals saved as separate assets

a useful implementation prompt:

> build the approved mockup as a responsive page
> preserve its layout, spacing, typography and visual hierarchy, use the approved copy and implement the interactions we agreed
> flag anything that needs a design decision before changing it

7. compare the rendered website with the mockup

have Codex open the implemented page in a browser and capture screenshots at desktop and mobile sizes

compare those screenshots with the approved design and work through the differences

check spacing, font sizes, image proportions, alignment and text wrapping, then test the links, forms and keyboard navigation

after you've reviewed the page, save the final screenshots and reusable design rules with the project for the next page you build

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

[📃 PAPER ALERT] Efficient, Property-Aligned Fan-Out Retrieval via RL-Compiled Diffusion - by Google Research & UIUC
arXiv: https://t.co/tt5pGCsbU3

When we search something broad like “camping gear,” we don't really want 10 slightly different tents.

We want:
tent + sleeping bag + stove + headlamp + other complementary things.
So modern search systems use query fan-out: take one broad query --> generate multiple sub-queries --> retrieve different aspects of the user's intent.

Sounds simple.

But there is a problem.

LLMs are autoregressive. To generate a good set of complementary, diverse AND database-grounded queries, they may need expensive inference-time reasoning.

And for a search system... do we really want the model to “think” heavily every single time someone searches?

I think NO.

This paper proposes : Retrieve-for-Train.

The idea is actually quite interesting:

Use expensive RL during TRAINING, not during INFERENCE.

The pipeline has 3 stages:

Train a Fan-Out Language Model (FOLM) using RL to generate useful sub-queries.

The reward jointly optimizes:

a. Groundedness: are the queries actually connected to items in the database?
b. Alignment: do they still follow the user's original intent?
c. Diversity: do they explore genuinely different semantic directions?

Use this RL-trained model to generate synthetic supervision.
So the expensive exploration happens offline.
No human-labelled property-aligned dataset is required.

Train a lightweight diffusion retriever on these generated targets.

At inference time, instead of autoregressively generating query after query...

the diffusion model generates multiple retrieval directions in parallel in embedding space.

Basically:

RL discovers the search strategy --> synthetic data stores it --> diffusion executes it cheaply.

Findings:
1. Zero-shot query fan-out helps, but it is not enough.
Normal LLMs often generate near-identical queries.
R4T instead learns complementary directions that cover more of the semantic space.
2. R4T improves retrieval quality over zero-shot fan-out and Best-of-N baselines.
The method was evaluated on fashion and music retrieval tasks where the desired output is a set rather than one correct item.
3. The diffusion retriever makes fan-out dramatically cheaper.

Their 53.9M-parameter diffusion model generates the retrieval directions non-autoregressively.

Reported fan-out latency:

LLM: ~1.46 s → ~50 s as batch size grows
Diffusion: ~0.07 s → 4.21 s

That is roughly 12×–20× faster.

[Interestingly]
The diversity reward is doing something more important than simply making the results diverse.

Without it, the RL model can reward-hack.

Optimizing only groundedness can produce nonsense strings that happen to land close to database embeddings.
Adding alignment alone can instead make the model collapse into repetitive paraphrases.

Groundedness + Alignment + Diversity work like counter-anchors that prevent these shortcuts.

I found this part particularly interesting because it shows how important reward interaction is in RL-based retrieval.

[In short] Instead of asking a large model to solve the same difficult search problem again and again at inference time...solve it during training and compile the learned behavior into a smaller model.

So the idea is almost:
System-2-like exploration during training → System-1-like retrieval during deployment.
And I think the broader idea may be even more interesting than retrieval itself.
Can we use RL to discover expensive behaviors once, turn those behaviors into training data, and then deploy a much cheaper model that reproduces them?

It’s funny because when I first got really deep into generative AI, I was basically a hardcore Midjourney user. Some of my earliest followers probably still remember that.

Back then, I never seriously thought I would end up making micro-drama series with AI. Video model capabilities were still extremely limited and most AI films followed a similar format: generate a bunch of interesting shots, edit them together, then add a voiceover to make everything feel connected.

Nothing wrong with that. It just wasn’t what I wanted to make.

I wanted actual scenes. Characters talking to each other. Dialogue, comedy, mise en scene, recurring characters and some kind of continuity. I wanted to see what happened when two characters were left in a room together, not just make a montage of beautiful images.

For quite some time, the technology simply couldn’t do that reliably. The face would change, the room would change, the performance wouldn’t land or the character would suddenly become a completely different person halfway through the shot.

Then Seedance 2.0 came out and I remember thinking, damnnn, maybe I can actually do this now.

That was really the beginning of SARI & PLOY.

I had all these ideas inspired by things around me. Jakarta, Bangkok, schoolcore aesthetic, night markets, rave spaces, cheap rented rooms, neighborhood gossip, local action films, street fashion, stupid jokes and all the other things that somehow live together in my head.

Most of them would be difficult, expensive or honestly just too weird and unnecessary to produce traditionally. I can’t imagine trying to explain some of this stuff in a commercial production meeting.

But with AI, I could just try it.

I’m not doing this because I want to “revolutionize filmmaking” or make some grand statement about the future of cinema. I just finally found a way to make ideas that probably wouldn’t survive a commercial brief.

And somewhere along the way, Sari, Ploy, Sekar, Busaba and the rest of them started becoming a real part of my everyday life.

I do my normal work, go home and then start thinking about what happens to them next. What kind of trouble they get into. What Mamet sees through that stupid camera on his collar. What the next corner of their world should look like.

That part was unexpected. I thought I was experimenting with a new medium. I didn’t expect to become this attached to the characters.

I guess that’s also why MXVDXN has started making more sense to me as its own thing. A place for the ideas that are too weird, too regional, too niche, too sensual, too violent, too impractical or simply too unnecessary for my normal commercial work.

The technology will probably keep getting more expensive, which is challenging.

But right now, I’m having way too much fun making this world exist. I genuinely look forward to going home and continuing it. That’s enough reason for me to keep going.

Qwen released Qwen-Image-2.1.

A new open-weight AI model that can create and edit images in one workflow.

It can:

• Generate images from text
• Edit images using up to 10 reference images
• Make precise edits while preserving details
• Generate transparent images natively
• Create infographics, storyboards and panoramas
• Handle text inside images
• Run through Hugging Face, Diffusers and ComfyUI

But there’s a catch:

You own the content you generate, but the model weights are under a research license.

So, open-weight doesn’t automatically mean free for commercial use. Developers using the weights commercially may need a separate license.

Qwen is making image generation more open, but the licensing details matter.
